title: Syllables and accent

objectives.can: Divide a Latin word into syllables and place its accent by the rule of the penult.

explanation.summary: A Latin word has as many syllables as it has vowels and diphthongs, and its accent falls by a simple rule that looks at the last three syllables. Knowing the rule lets you say any word aloud, in either pronunciation, and it explains why a word such as *Dominus* is stressed on its first syllable.

sections.heading: Counting syllables
body: Each vowel or diphthong makes one syllable. The diphthongs you will meet are ae (printed æ in this edition), oe and au, and, rarely, ei, eu and ui. So *cælum* has two syllables (*cæ-lum*), *tenebræ* has three (*te-ne-bræ*), and *causa* has two, because au counts as one vowel.

Two vowels side by side that are not a diphthong make two syllables: *Deus* is *De-us* and *gloriam* is *glo-ri-am*. The letter u after q or g belongs to the consonant, not to a syllable of its own, so *aquas* is *a-quas*, two syllables. Between two vowels the letter i (printed j in this edition, as in *ejus*) is a consonant and does not make a syllable.

sections.heading: Dividing words
body: A single consonant between two vowels goes with the vowel after it: *do-mi-nus*, *lu-cem*. When two consonants come together, the syllable break falls between them: *ver-bum*, *ter-ram*. A stop (p, b, t, d, c, g) followed by l or r usually stays together and begins the next syllable: *te-ne-bræ*. The letter x counts as two consonants (c and s), so the break falls inside it: *re-sur-rex-it*. This division matters because it tells you whether a syllable is long by position, as the next section explains.

sections.heading: The rule of the penult
body: The penult is the next-to-last syllable and the antepenult the one before it. The accent obeys three steps. A word of two syllables is accented on the first (*VER-bum*, *DE-us*). In a longer word the accent falls on the penult if the penult is long, and otherwise on the antepenult.

A penult is long if it contains a long vowel or a diphthong, or if its vowel is followed by two consonants (or x). So the accent of *re-sur-REX-it* falls on rex, long by position, but the accent of *DO-mi-nus* falls on do, because the penult mi has a short vowel followed by a single consonant. The accent is a stress that the reader gives the syllable; it is never printed in the text, and it is never part of the spelling.

sections.heading: Long and short vowels
body: A long vowel is held about twice as long as a short one. The classical pronunciation keeps the difference, and the rule of the penult depends on it, but the editions in this library print no macrons. So the penult rule cannot always be applied by sight. Where the penult is closed by two consonants, or contains a diphthong, you can see it is long. Otherwise you need the common patterns, which this lesson states as they come: the perfect ending -avit and the endings -orum and -arum have a long vowel; the ending -itas, as in *veritas*, has a short i.
A dictionary for learners marks length; the Vulgate edition here does not. Treat the patterns above as guides and not as a complete list.

sections.heading: Words with -que, -ne and -ve
body: The small words *-que* ('and'), *-ne* (the question marker) and *-ve* ('or') attach to the end of another word and are called enclitics. They are not accented themselves; they pull the accent onto the last syllable of the word they join, whatever its quantity. *Dixit* is accented DIX-it, but *Dixitque* is accented dix-IT-que. The same holds of *Appellavitque* in Genesis 1:5, accented on the syllable before the -que.

misunderstandings: The ligature æ is one vowel sound, not two: *cælum* has two syllables, not three. Likewise au in *causa* is one syllable.
*Deus* is not a diphthong word. Its e and u are two vowels in two syllables, *De-us*, and the accent falls on the first.
The penult is the second-last syllable, not the second-last letter, and not the second syllable of a long word. Count from the end.
The accent rule does not say a vowel is long because the accent falls on it. It says the accent falls on the penult if the penult is long. Length comes first, and the accent follows it.

deeper.heading: Accent and quantity
body: Roman grammarians described the Latin accent as a rise in pitch, and classical verse was built on the pattern of long and short syllables, not on stress. By late antiquity the accent had become more a matter of stress, and medieval hymns are built on stress. The ecclesiastical pronunciation gives the accent as stress. The rule of the penult is the same in both traditions.

examples.analysis: *creavit* has three syllables, *cre-a-vit*. The penult a is long, as in every perfect in -avit, so the accent falls on it: *cre-A-vit*. The ea is not a diphthong in Latin.

examples.analysis: *Dixitque* is *Dixit* with the enclitic *-que*. *Dixit* alone is accented on its first syllable, DIX-it. With *-que* the accent moves to the syllable before it: *dix-IT-que*. The x makes the break fall inside it, *dix-it*.

check.prompt: Which of these makes a penult long?
options: Its vowel is followed by two consonants
It has a vowel and no consonant
It comes before the enclitic -que only
It is the first syllable of the word
check.explain: A penult is long by a long vowel, by a diphthong or by position, that is, a vowel followed by two consonants or x. The other statements are not rules.
